albums.blurb: Christian Fennesz is an Austrian guitarist and laptop composer, the best-known artist on Vienna's Mego label, who later recorded duo albums with Ryuichi Sakamoto. Endless Summer (2001) is his third album and the center of his catalogue: electric guitar processed through granular software into a warm haze, with surf- and pop-inflected melodies surfacing through the static — a deliberate melodic turn after the harsher Hotel Paral.lel. All ten tracks are instrumental, and Editions Mego reissued the album in 2006 with additional material.
albums.reception: Pitchfork rated it 9.4/10 on release, and Exclaim! called it the electronic album of the year for 2001.

albums.blurb: Before Loving in Stereo, the London production duo of Josh Lloyd-Watson and Tom McFarland released this self-titled debut on XL Recordings in July 2014, back when they kept their identities hidden behind the initials J and T. Its twelve tracks of falsetto-led, midtempo 1970s-styled funk and soul — including the early singles Busy Earnin' and The Heat — set the template the band has elaborated on every record since.
albums.reception: The album was shortlisted for the 2014 Mercury Prize and reached No. 7 on the UK Albums Chart.

albums.blurb: Duster are a San Jose trio — Clay Parton, Canaan Dove Amber and Jason Albertini — who recorded this debut for Up Records on cheap four-track equipment in 1998. Its seventeen short pieces drift between slow, murmured songs and hazy instrumentals, a sound since filed under slowcore and space rock. The band released one more album, Contemporary Movement (2000), then went quiet for nearly two decades before a 2019 reunion.
albums.reception: Largely unnoticed on release, it became a collector's item — original vinyl copies traded for over $400 — and Pitchfork gave it a retrospective 8.6 around Numero Group's 2019 reissue of the band's catalogue.
